before: The command-line interface, or CLI, runs a PHP source file from a terminal. Save the complete example as main.php and run php main.php with a local PHP installation.
<?php begins PHP code. A file containing only PHP normally omits the closing tag so accidental trailing text is not sent as output.

This course verifies PHP 8.5.12 CLI examples. A terminal run does not demonstrate browser-cookie behavior, deployed server headers or connections to an external production database. Local session storage and in-memory database tests are separate capabilities when their extensions are installed.
Running php main.php reads the current file in this ordinary CLI workflow. It is not the separate manual compilation workflow used in C. The app itself does not run PHP.

Complete local PHP example; the app itself does not execute it:
```php
<?php
echo "Ready\n";

```
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Run the file twice with a changed message. Distinguish terminal output from an HTTP response. You may trace it without a PHP interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A PHP interpreter reads PHP instructions and runs them.
A terminal is a place to type commands. This example sends its message there.
If PHP is installed, save the file as main.php and run php main.php from its folder. A web server is not needed here.
When PHP runs this file, it shows the word that is saved inside the quotes.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```php
<?php
echo "Ready\n";
```
The output is `Ready`. The command reads the saved file on this run.
